## Proof

Let $f(z)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n z^n$ be holomorphic and injective on $D(0,R)^\circ$. Since $f$ is injective and holomorphic, $f'(z)\neq 0$ for all $z\in D(0,R)^\circ$ (a standard consequence of the local form of a holomorphic map: a zero of $f'$ would make $f$ locally $k$-to-one with $k\ge 2$). Fix $r\in(0,R)$.

---

### (b) Area formula $A(r)=\pi\sum_{n=1}^\infty n|c_n|^2 r^{2n}$

Since $f$ is injective on $D(0,r)\subset D(0,R)^\circ$, the change-of-variables formula gives

$$A(r)=\operatorname{area}\bigl(f(D(0,r))\bigr)=\iint_{D(0,r)}|f'(z)|^2\,dA(z).$$

(The Jacobian determinant of the holomorphic map $f$ is $|f'(z)|^2$.) Writing $z=\rho e^{i\theta}$,

$$A(r)=\int_0^r\!\int_0^{2\pi}|f'(\rho e^{i\theta})|^2\,\rho\,d\theta\,d\rho.$$

Now $f'(z)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty n c_n z^{n-1}$, converging uniformly on compact subsets of $D(0,R)^\circ$, hence uniformly on $\overline{D(0,r)}$. Thus

$$|f'(\rho e^{i\theta})|^2=\Bigl(\sum_{n=1}^\infty n c_n \rho^{n-1}e^{i(n-1)\theta}\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_{m=1}^\infty m\overline{c_m}\rho^{m-1}e^{-i(m-1)\theta}\Bigr)=\sum_{n,m\ge 1}nm\,c_n\overline{c_m}\,\rho^{n+m-2}e^{i(n-m)\theta},$$

and the series converges uniformly on $[0,r]\times[0,2\pi]$, so we may integrate termwise. Using

$$\int_0^{2\pi}e^{i(n-m)\theta}\,d\theta=2\pi\,\delta_{nm},$$

we obtain

$$\int_0^{2\pi}|f'(\rho e^{i\theta})|^2\,d\theta=2\pi\sum_{n=1}^\infty n^2|c_n|^2\rho^{2n-2}.$$

Therefore

$$A(r)=\int_0^r 2\pi\sum_{n=1}^\infty n^2|c_n|^2\rho^{2n-2}\,\rho\,d\rho=2\pi\sum_{n=1}^\infty n^2|c_n|^2\int_0^r\rho^{2n-1}\,d\rho=2\pi\sum_{n=1}^\infty n^2|c_n|^2\cdot\frac{r^{2n}}{2n}=\pi\sum_{n=1}^\infty n|c_n|^2 r^{2n}.$$

This proves **(b)**.

---

### (c) Area lower bound $A(r)\ge \pi r^2|f'(0)|^2$

From (b),

$$A(r)=\pi\sum_{n=1}^\infty n|c_n|^2 r^{2n}.$$

Every term in the sum is non-negative, so dropping all terms with $n\ge 2$ only decreases the value:

$$A(r)\ge \pi\cdot 1\cdot|c_1|^2 r^2=\pi r^2|c_1|^2.$$

Since $c_1=f'(0)$, we conclude

$$A(r)\ge \pi r^2|f'(0)|^2.$$

This proves **(c)**.

---

### (a) Length lower bound $L(r)\ge 2\pi r|f'(0)|$

The circle $\partial D(0,r)$ is parametrized by $\gamma(\theta)=re^{i\theta}$, $\theta\in[0,2\pi]$, with $|\gamma'(\theta)|=r$. The image curve $f\circ\gamma$ has length

$$L(r)=\int_0^{2\pi}|(f\circ\gamma)'(\theta)|\,d\theta=\int_0^{2\pi}|f'(re^{i\theta})|\,r\,d\theta=r\int_0^{2\pi}|f'(re^{i\theta})|\,d\theta.$$

(For injective $f$ this is exactly the length of the Jordan curve $f(\partial D(0,r))$.)

Now $f'$ is holomorphic on $D(0,R)^\circ$, so by the mean-value property (Cauchy's integral formula applied to $f'$ at $0$, with the circle of radius $r$),

$$f'(0)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}f'(re^{i\theta})\,d\theta.$$

Applying the triangle inequality for integrals,

$$|f'(0)|=\left|\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}f'(re^{i\theta})\,d\theta\right|\le\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|f'(re^{i\theta})|\,d\theta.$$

Multiplying both sides by $2\pi r>0$,

$$2\pi r\,|f'(0)|\le r\int_0^{2\pi}|f'(re^{i\theta})|\,d\theta=L(r).$$

This proves **(a)**.

---

All three parts are established. Note that (a) relies only on the mean-value property of the holomorphic function $f'$, while (b) uses injectivity to apply the area formula, and (c) is an immediate consequence of (b) together with the non-negativity of every term in the series.
